stories.title: Biju Rao's Village Experience
stories.description: Amit recounts a story from Biju Rao's fieldwork. While interviewing women in a village, a husband dragged his wife out by her hair for talking to the researchers. Later, after building trust, the women revealed they felt like they were in 'jail' and that domestic violence was a rational choice by husbands to extract money from the wife's family.

stories.title: Charles Booth's London
stories.description: Amit discusses Charles Booth's monumental 17-year study 'Life and Labour of the People of London', which combined quantitative data and qualitative observation to create a rich picture of London life, before the social sciences split into silos.

stories.title: Ajay's Mall Walk
stories.description: Ajay recounts a 'peak experience' where he spent four hours walking in a mall with the head of marketing of a garments firm, learning about the business from the ground up.

core_ideas.item: Read Books for Ideas, Papers for Techniques
core_ideas.description: Ed Glaeser's advice. Books allow for world-building and big ideas, while papers are for rigorous, narrow arguments. Both are necessary.
The ability to see others as they see themselves, rather than projecting one's own feelings or frameworks onto them. Essential for understanding social phenomena.
Taking words seriously, not just numbers. Stories and qualitative data reveal the 'why' behind the 'what' that numbers measure.
Quantitative economics often relies on snapshots (before/after), whereas ethnography allows for observing the process of change as it happens over time.
Ethnography has high internal validity (true for this specific context) but low external validity (hard to generalize). Quantitative methods often have the reverse. We need both.
Ajay warns against papers with grandiose titles that don't specify their narrow context (e.g., 'The Effect of X on Y' vs 'The Effect of X on Y in Rural Tamil Nadu').
Reading should be an active conversation/argument with the author, not passive consumption. This leads to better retention and understanding.
